title: Attention, Hyperactivity-Impulsivity and Study Disposition in Adolescents in Foster Care and Families of Origin: A Multi-Informant Study of Relational Trauma and Protective Resources
content: Background/Objectives: Relational trauma may increase the risk of attentional and behavioral difficulties during adolescence, which may, in turn, interfere with engagement in studying. However, poorer adjustment should not be attributed to foster care itself without considering previous adversity and protective resources. This study examined attention problems, hyperactivity-impulsivity, and study disposition in adolescents in foster care and adolescents living with their families of origin, considering relational trauma, perceived social support, resilience, and stress management. Methods: Participants were 32 adolescent–caregiver dyads from Spain, comprising 16 adolescents in foster care and their caregivers and 16 adolescents living with their families of origin and their caregivers. Adolescents were aged 12–19 years. A multi-informant assessment included both adolescent self-report and caregiver-report measures. Outcomes and protective factors were assessed using the SENA (Attention, Hyperactivity-Impulsivity and Attitudes towards Studying), CaMir (Relational Trauma), EQ-i:YV (Stress management), CD-RISC-10 (Resilience), and MOS Social Support Survey (Social Suport). Data were analyzed using group comparisons, ANCOVAs, MANCOVAs, and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA). Results: Adolescents in foster care reported significantly higher levels of relational trauma than those living with their families of origin. Across both adolescent and caregiver reports, higher relational trauma was associated with greater attention problems and hyperactivity-impulsivity, whereas foster-care status itself was not associated with these difficulties after relational trauma was considered. Neither relational trauma nor resilience was independently associated with study disposition. Regarding protective factors, perceived social support was not significantly associated with attention or hyperactivity-impulsivity, whereas better stress management was associated with fewer self-reported attention problems and hyperactivity-impulsivity. Finally, fsQCA showed that poor stress management frequently characterized configurations associated with greater attention and hyperactivity-impulsivity problems, whereas the absence of relational trauma combined with protective resources, particularly resilience or good stress management, characterized more favorable adjustment profiles. Higher study disposition was also observed in configurations combining resilience with the absence of relational trauma. Conclusions: Relational trauma may be more informative than current family placement for understanding attentional and behavioral difficulties, while protective resources may operate mainly in combination rather than in isolation.
